The fourth‑largest city in Germany is **Cologne** (Köln).  
Its original Roman name was **_Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium_** – the Latin designation given when the Romans founded the settlement on the Rhine in the 1st century AD.

Thus, the city we now call Cologne was originally called **Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium**.

Along the banks of the Rhine River, Köln stands as a testament to Germany’s rich heritage and vibrant spirit. From its awe-inspiring landmarks to its eclectic arts scene and culinary delights, Köln offers a captivating blend of history, culture, and modernity.
Many people do not know where the name “Köln” came from, and i am here to clear that out for you.
Köln is derived from the Latin name “Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium.” This Latin name was given to the city by the Romans when they established a settlement there around 50 AD. The term “Colonia” referred to a Roman settlement or colony, while “Claudia” honored the Roman Emperor Claudius, and “Ara Agrippinensium” referenced the local tribe, the Agrippinenses, and their shrine to the Celtic goddess Ara.

Title: Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium
Chunks: 0,1,2
For sure, our year of 2017 was fully dedicated to travels from the south to the north and back. After having changed a variety of landscapes and architecture, culture and history, food and low-alcoholic drinks (like beer and wine) in several Scandinavian and Mediterranean countries several times, we came back to the north again. We said bye-bye to the Greek**Lady of the North and Bride of the Thermaic Gulf** and headed for the colony of _Julia Augusta Agrippina Minor_ (or better known as _Agrippina the Younger_), i.e. we made one journey to Germany and our first stop was in ….
**C O L O G N E**
_Köln_ is the German name of the fourth largest city of Deutschland (Germany) after Berlin, Hamburg and München. It is situated in the North Rhine-Westphalia which is the most populous federal state of the country. It’s a crossroad and one of the most developed and urbanized areas of Germany and Europe. The reasons for that is its location in the Rhine-Ruhr region where mining, timber and logging, and heavy industries are strongly developed. Apart from this, the Rhine River which is one of the major and leading navigable waterways in Europe predisposes the development of the river cargo transport. Last but not least, the city is full of history with origin dating back to the Roman period.
A settlement called _Oppidum Ubiorum_ was founded by the ancient Romans in the 1 st century BC and later it was named after _Emperor Claudius’_ wife _Agrippina_. It was established as a boundary after the Roman plans of conquering _Greater Germania_ had been abandoned and the Roman settlement had been made a colony in the Rhineland bearing its new name, i.e. _CCAA_ (_Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium_). Then the town developed greatly in the middle ages. Unfortunately, the city of Cologne was bombarded and almost fully destroyed like most of the German cities during the World War II and later it was fully reconstructed.
Nowadays the city of Cologne is one of the most visited places in the country and of course, every exploration of the city starts from its emblematic **Kölner Dom** (Cologne Cathedral). When you get out of the Köln _Hauptbahnhof_ (the Central Station) you bump up into the immense holy building whose construction took about seven centuries.

The enormous building is about 144 meters long and 86 meters wide. As to its height …. Woooow …. Its north tower is around 157 meters high and it is only 7 centimeters higher than the south one. It was the tallest building in the world for four years (1880 – 1884). Today the Cathedral ranks second after the tallest telecommunications towers of Cologne. By the way, it’s an interesting fact that the Holy Building never fell although it was hit by 14 bombs during the WWII. And do you know why? Because it’s believed to have been a very easily recognizable landmark for pilots.
Well, for the time-being we are postponing the visit to **Kölner Dom**for a little bit later and we are getting back to the “Roman Empire”. Are you asking me how? Trust me, I will teleport you back to the Roman times but please, note that journey back to history will be a little bit odd and weird. I am saying it now and I will repeat it later too – don’t consider the two paragraphs below an insult or any of kind of offense. Nope, it’s not. This is just a moment from our trip shared with all of you.
Sooooo …. Ladies and Gentlemen, let me invite you to one of my boyfriend’s houses along the Rhine and especially, in Cologne, i.e. to the **_Roman-Germanic Museum_**. He – _Sergio Primus Germanicus_, as an authentic representative of the Roman Empire, will welcome you to his 3 rd century town villa and you will sit for a while in “his living-room” with Dionysus mosaics for a glass of nice wine from the Rhine region which was very famous and highly appreciated in the Roman Empire. Then he will walk you through the other parts of his villa plus he will show you the ancient Roman carriage with which he obtained his driving license.

But it won’t be the end of your visit of _il capoluogo_(the main town) of the ancient Roman province of Lower Germania. _Sergio Primus Germanicus_ will introduce you to the Imperial Governor of Cologne in his official residence, i.e. in _the **Praetorium**_. At the end of the visit, he will accompany you to the town gate to the north where you will see the inscription CCAA which will show you exactly where you are, i.e. in _Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium_.
Well, guys, this is simply a joke. I don’t want to offend anybody, to underestimate anything or to sound unserious (if so, please, accept my sincere apologies) but I can assure you that the _Römisch-Germanisches_ _Museum_ and the _Praetorium_(in German) are very familiar especially to the Italians because they find lots of artifacts, glassware and mosaics which date back to the Roman Empire. Moreover, they feel “at home” (as my boyfriend said when we were there) and while paying a visit to both archeological sites they link them both to their ancestors and their everyday life in a very entertaining way and with much sense of humour. 🙂
If you already want we can come back to today’s city of Cologne again. Nope. let us first go through the medieval era and visit **Kölner Dom**.

Along the banks of the Rhine River, Köln stands as a testament to Germany’s rich heritage and vibrant spirit. From its awe-inspiring landmarks to its eclectic arts scene and culinary delights, Köln offers a captivating blend of history, culture, and modernity.
Many people do not know where the name “Köln” came from, and i am here to clear that out for you.
Köln is derived from the Latin name “Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium.” This Latin name was given to the city by the Romans when they established a settlement there around 50 AD. The term “Colonia” referred to a Roman settlement or colony, while “Claudia” honored the Roman Emperor Claudius, and “Ara Agrippinensium” referenced the local tribe, the Agrippinenses, and their shrine to the Celtic goddess Ara.
So, after understanding the origin of its name, join me and let us embark on a journey through the heart of this dynamic city through some photographs i had taken on my first ever visit to Köln:
> The Cologne Cathedral:  
>   
>   
> Dominating the skyline with its majestic spires, the Cologne Cathedral is a masterpiece of Gothic architecture and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

For sure, our year of 2017 was fully dedicated to travels from the south to the north and back. After having changed a variety of landscapes and architecture, culture and history, food and low-alcoholic drinks (like beer and wine) in several Scandinavian and Mediterranean countries several times, we came back to the north again. We said bye-bye to the Greek**Lady of the North and Bride of the Thermaic Gulf** and headed for the colony of _Julia Augusta Agrippina Minor_ (or better known as _Agrippina the Younger_), i.e. we made one journey to Germany and our first stop was in ….
**C O L O G N E**
_Köln_ is the German name of the fourth largest city of Deutschland (Germany) after Berlin, Hamburg and München. It is situated in the North Rhine-Westphalia which is the most populous federal state of the country. It’s a crossroad and one of the most developed and urbanized areas of Germany and Europe. The reasons for that is its location in the Rhine-Ruhr region where mining, timber and logging, and heavy industries are strongly developed. Apart from this, the Rhine River which is one of the major and leading navigable waterways in Europe predisposes the development of the river cargo transport. Last but not least, the city is full of history with origin dating back to the Roman period.
A settlement called _Oppidum Ubiorum_ was founded by the ancient Romans in the 1 st century BC and later it was named after _Emperor Claudius’_ wife _Agrippina_. It was established as a boundary after the Roman plans of conquering _Greater Germania_ had been abandoned and the Roman settlement had been made a colony in the Rhineland bearing its new name, i.e. _CCAA_ (_Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium_). Then the town developed greatly in the middle ages. Unfortunately, the city of Cologne was bombarded and almost fully destroyed like most of the German cities during the World War II and later it was fully reconstructed.
Nowadays the city of Cologne is one of the most visited places in the country and of course, every exploration of the city starts from its emblematic **Kölner Dom** (Cologne Cathedral). When you get out of the Köln _Hauptbahnhof_ (the Central Station) you bump up into the immense holy building whose construction took about seven centuries.
texts.1:
The enormous building is about 144 meters long and 86 meters wide. As to its height …. Woooow …. Its north tower is around 157 meters high and it is only 7 centimeters higher than the south one. It was the tallest building in the world for four years (1880 – 1884). Today the Cathedral ranks second after the tallest telecommunications towers of Cologne. By the way, it’s an interesting fact that the Holy Building never fell although it was hit by 14 bombs during the WWII. And do you know why? Because it’s believed to have been a very easily recognizable landmark for pilots.
Well, for the time-being we are postponing the visit to **Kölner Dom**for a little bit later and we are getting back to the “Roman Empire”. Are you asking me how? Trust me, I will teleport you back to the Roman times but please, note that journey back to history will be a little bit odd and weird. I am saying it now and I will repeat it later too – don’t consider the two paragraphs below an insult or any of kind of offense. Nope, it’s not. This is just a moment from our trip shared with all of you.
Sooooo …. Ladies and Gentlemen, let me invite you to one of my boyfriend’s houses along the Rhine and especially, in Cologne, i.e. to the **_Roman-Germanic Museum_**. He – _Sergio Primus Germanicus_, as an authentic representative of the Roman Empire, will welcome you to his 3 rd century town villa and you will sit for a while in “his living-room” with Dionysus mosaics for a glass of nice wine from the Rhine region which was very famous and highly appreciated in the Roman Empire. Then he will walk you through the other parts of his villa plus he will show you the ancient Roman carriage with which he obtained his driving license.
texts.2:
But it won’t be the end of your visit of _il capoluogo_(the main town) of the ancient Roman province of Lower Germania. _Sergio Primus Germanicus_ will introduce you to the Imperial Governor of Cologne in his official residence, i.e. in _the **Praetorium**_. At the end of the visit, he will accompany you to the town gate to the north where you will see the inscription CCAA which will show you exactly where you are, i.e. in _Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium_.
Well, guys, this is simply a joke. I don’t want to offend anybody, to underestimate anything or to sound unserious (if so, please, accept my sincere apologies) but I can assure you that the _Römisch-Germanisches_ _Museum_ and the _Praetorium_(in German) are very familiar especially to the Italians because they find lots of artifacts, glassware and mosaics which date back to the Roman Empire. Moreover, they feel “at home” (as my boyfriend said when we were there) and while paying a visit to both archeological sites they link them both to their ancestors and their everyday life in a very entertaining way and with much sense of humour. 🙂
If you already want we can come back to today’s city of Cologne again. Nope. let us first go through the medieval era and visit **Kölner Dom**.
